section_title: What changes when Israel turns back to the LORD?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Then the men of Kiriath-jearim came for the ark of the LORD and took it into Abinadab’s house on the hill. And they consecrated his son Eleazar to guard the ark of the LORD. 2 And from that day a long time passed, twenty years in all, as the ark remained at Kiriath-jearim. And all the house of Israel mournfully sought the LORD. 3 Then Samuel said to all the house of Israel, “If you are returning to the LORD with all your hearts, then put away the foreign gods and Ashtoreths among you, prepare your hearts for the LORD, and serve Him only. And He will deliver you from the hand of the Philistines.” 4 So the Israelites put away the Baals and Ashtoreths and served only the LORD.

5 Then Samuel said, “Gather all Israel to Mizpah, and I will pray to the LORD on your behalf.” 6 When they had gathered at Mizpah, they drew water and poured it out before the LORD. On that day they fasted, and there they confessed, “We have sinned against the LORD.” And Samuel judged the Israelites at Mizpah. 7 When the Philistines heard that the Israelites had gathered at Mizpah, their rulers marched up toward Israel. And when the Israelites learned of this, they feared the Philistines 8 and said to Samuel, “Do not stop crying out to the LORD our God for us, that He may save us from the hand of the Philistines.” 9 Then Samuel took a suckling lamb and offered it as a whole burnt offering to the LORD. He cried out to the LORD on behalf of Israel, and the LORD answered him.

10 As the Philistines drew near to fight against Israel, Samuel was offering up the burnt offering. But that day the LORD thundered loudly against the Philistines and threw them into such confusion that they fled before Israel. 11 Then the men of Israel charged out of Mizpah and pursued the Philistines, striking them down all the way to an area below Beth-car. 12 Afterward, Samuel took a stone and set it up between Mizpah and Shen. He named it Ebenezer, saying, “Thus far the LORD has helped us.” 13 So the Philistines were subdued, and they stopped invading the territory of Israel. And the hand of the LORD was against the Philistines all the days of Samuel. 14 The cities from Ekron to Gath, which the Philistines had taken, were restored to Israel, who also delivered the surrounding territory from the hand of the Philistines. And there was peace between the Israelites and the Amorites.

15 So Samuel judged Israel all the days of his life. 16 Every year he would go on a circuit from Bethel to Gilgal to Mizpah, judging Israel in all these places. 17 Then he would return to Ramah because his home was there, and there he judged Israel and built an altar to the LORD.

context_lines: The ark is taken to Abinadab’s house at Kiriath-jearim, and his son Eleazar is set apart to guard it. After twenty years, Israel is mournfully seeking the LORD. Samuel calls for a concrete response: put away foreign gods, direct their hearts to the LORD, and serve Him alone. The people remove the Baals and Ashtoreths.

At Mizpah they fast, pour out water before the LORD, and confess their sin. Samuel prays for them and acts as judge. When the Philistines approach, the people are afraid again. This time they ask Samuel to keep crying to God for rescue, rather than trying to secure victory by bringing the ark into battle.

Samuel offers a young lamb as a whole burnt offering and prays. The LORD answers with thunder that throws the Philistines into confusion. Israel pursues the fleeing army. The help comes from God, yet the text also describes the Israelites’ own action in the pursuit.

Samuel sets up a stone to remember the LORD’s help. The account describes restored territory and peace, then closes with his continuing work as judge. He travels a regular circuit and returns to Ramah, where he also builds an altar. The chapter joins a moment of deliverance with the steady work of governing and worshiping.
common_interpretation_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) and [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/7.htm) read the return to God as more than sorrow at the loss of the ark. Removing idols and confessing sin give substance to the people’s change. They understand the poured-out water as an expression of humility and repentance. The narrator records the action beside fasting and confession without prescribing it as a ritual every later believer must perform.

[Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/7.htm) likewise interprets the water in terms of repentance, distinguishing it from a celebration or an ordeal in which people drink it. He and Wesley also explain that the twenty years are not necessarily the whole time the ark remains at Kiriath-jearim. The verse marks the period leading into the events narrated here.

The description of Philistine restraint is read in light of later battles under Saul. [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/7.htm) understand it especially in relation to Samuel’s period of sole leadership, rather than claiming that no Philistine force ever appears again during his lifetime. Their reading preserves both this deliverance and the later narrative.
god_plan_lines: [Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-first-book-of-samuel/) and [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/7.htm) draw a Christian comparison from Samuel’s sacrifice and intercession. Samuel stands before God on behalf of a fearful people, and the LORD answers. The comparison directs attention to the greater intercessor described in [Hebrews 7:23–28](https://biblehub.com/bsb/hebrews/7.htm).

Hebrews explains the difference as well as the connection: Jesus lives forever, continually intercedes, and has offered Himself once for all. Samuel offers a lamb and asks for rescue from a particular enemy. Jesus’ priesthood supplies enduring access to God and salvation for those who draw near through Him. The shared pattern of intercession points beyond Samuel without making this battle the whole meaning of Christian salvation.
